speaker: John Quinn
title: Ep 110 | John B. Quinn | Big Law Litigation Trailblazer & Pioneer
question: In corporate legal services, what actually determines whether a law firm keeps a major client for decades?
guest: Well, look, clients are personal relationships. Our clients are typically in-house lawyers—they might be a general counsel, or an in-house lawyer who has responsibility for managing litigation—and it's that relationship that is the relationship between our firm and the client. Those relationships can change. Even though you've done fabulous work, there's a change in personnel: a new lawyer comes in, and they have their own historic relationships with other lawyers they've worked with in the past. So sometimes, despite your own best efforts and a great record, you end up finding the relationship becomes more and more attenuated, and eventually you're not representing that client anymore just because of a change in personnel. So if you're going to keep a client for decades, you have to be forming those personal relationships with different people, because people move and they change, and you have to win and reinforce that relationship all the time.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Long-term retention is determined less by legal brilliance than by the depth and breadth of the relationship. Technical excellence is assumed; it gets a firm hired but rarely keeps it.

What matters most is that the relationship is institutional rather than personal. Firms that hold clients for decades build ties across multiple partners, practice areas and seniority levels, so the relationship survives when a key partner retires or leaves, or when the general counsel changes. A new general counsel is the single most common trigger for losing a client, since they often bring their own trusted advisers.

The second factor is accumulated knowledge of the client's business, people, risk appetite and history. This creates real switching costs and lets the firm give commercial, practical advice rather than abstract legal analysis.

The third is service quality as the client experiences it: responsiveness, no surprises on bills, perceived value for money, and avoiding conflicts with the client's interests.

Finally, durable firms manage succession deliberately, introducing younger partners early, and stay on the client's panel by adapting to pricing pressure and the growth of in-house teams.

models.answer: Technical legal excellence is merely table stakes; keeping a major corporate client for decades depends on institutionalizing the relationship beyond any single individual. Over twenty or thirty years, partner retirements and general counsel turnover are inevitable, so ties anchored to one rainmaker rarely survive generational transitions. Enduring firms deliberately build multi-tiered relationships—pairing rising partners with future in-house leaders early—and collaborate across practice areas, which embeds institutional memory into the client’s operations and creates genuine switching costs. Equally decisive is commercial fluency: long-tenured firms internalize the client’s strategy, internal politics, and specific risk tolerance to deliver actionable business judgment rather than defensive legal caveats. Finally, multi-decade retention hinges on operational trust and active reinvention. Firms that last avoid billing surprises, own mistakes candidly, perform reliably during bet-the-company crises, and willingly adapt staffing and fee structures as new corporate leaders reevaluate incumbent counsel—never mistaking past loyalty for permanent security.

Usually it isn't technical brilliance. Large clients assume all top firms are competent, so excellence in legal work is the price of entry, not what keeps them. Client surveys from BTI Consulting and Thomson Reuters (formerly Acritas) consistently find that clients leave over service failures, like poor responsiveness, surprise bills, or a firm not understanding their business, much more often than over legal mistakes or price.

Lasting relationships rest on a few structural things. The relationship has to belong to the firm, not one partner. Several partners, ideally across several practice areas, need real ties at several levels of the client, so it survives retirements and lateral moves. Firms also have to plan handovers deliberately, because client turnover tends to follow changes on either side: a new general counsel often brings their own preferred firms, and a departing partner often takes the client along. Built-up knowledge of the client's history, people and risks makes switching costly. Above all, a firm keeps a client for decades by performing in the crises that put the company at stake and by acting like a business adviser who thinks ahead, not a vendor that bills by the hour.

Keeping a major corporate client for decades depends far more on institutionalizing the relationship than on any single lawyer’s brilliance or past wins. Technical excellence is merely table stakes; what creates lasting loyalty is deep, accumulated knowledge of the client’s business model, industry, internal politics, and risk tolerance. When outside counsel consistently translates complex law into practical, commercial judgment and anticipates problems before they become crises, the firm becomes a trusted strategic partner rather than an interchangeable vendor, creating natural switching costs that competitors struggle to overcome.

Just as critical is breadth and continuity. Multi-decade relationships survive because they are woven across multiple practice areas, geographies, and generations of leaders on both sides. Firms that rely on a single rainmaker lose clients when that partner retires or leaves, or when a new general counsel takes over. By deliberately embedding rising partners, investing in succession, delivering predictable value with transparent billing, and adapting as the client’s business evolves, a firm anchors the relationship to the institution rather than any individual.

A law firm keeps a major client for decades when successive general counsel can trust it with the next important matter. That trust comes from sound legal judgment, practical advice grounded in the client’s business, and reliable execution. The firm responds quickly, flags risks early, and explains what the work will cost and why. Thomson Reuters research found that value was the most frequently cited reason companies changed their law firm lineup, with work quality and responsiveness also among the reasons. [Thomson Reuters](https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/press-releases/2017/december/corporations-are-frequently-shuffling-their-law-firm-lineup)

Over decades, the test is whether that trust survives turnover on both sides. When several lawyers know the client’s business and history, a partner can retire or a new general counsel can take over without the relationship starting from scratch. That accumulated knowledge makes it easier to keep sending work to the firm, as long as the firm continues to deliver as the client’s needs change.

noweb.answer:
A law firm keeps a major client for decades by making it easy for successive general counsel to keep choosing it. That takes consistently good work, sound judgment under pressure, and a deep understanding of the client’s business. It also takes predictable fees, early warning when costs or risks change, and advice that helps executives make decisions.

The relationship is most vulnerable when a lead partner retires, a new general counsel arrives, or the client reviews its outside counsel. A firm that has earned trust across the legal department and developed several lawyers who know the business can carry that trust through a transition. The real test is whether the client would choose the firm again if the decision were made today.

A law firm keeps a major client for decades when the client’s legal team can repeatedly trust it with decisions that matter. Technical excellence earns the firm a place on the shortlist. What earns it the next call is knowing the business well enough to explain which risks matter, recommend a course of action, and flag bad news early. The client also needs to trust the firm’s judgment about cost, including when a problem deserves a smaller team or a less expensive solution.

For that trust to last decades, it has to survive turnover on both sides. A retiring partner’s successor has a better chance of keeping the work if the client has already seen that lawyer handle a difficult matter. And when a new general counsel arrives, the firm has to understand what the new leader needs. A long history is valuable because it builds knowledge and confidence. Each new assignment gives the client a reason to renew that confidence or reconsider it.
